Q: What is the best way to use Obsidian for vibe coding with GitHub and AI coding assistants? A:

llm-wiki approach - structured collection of doc files with index.md for hierarchical navigation looks like what you are looking for. Also you can use tags for connecting your code and docs - put same tag into doc and into code and that will allow AI to search doc by code or vice versa. Just put appropriate instructions into AGENTS.md and let AI maintain docs and tags.

Q: .md architecture for cursor agent optimization for my next projects A:

Putting all project documentation into a single `AGENTS.md` usually does not scale well, because it turns the file into a large context dump.

A many-small-docs approach can work better if the documents have clear ownership and navigation rules. One useful pattern is the llm-wiki idea from Andrej Karpathy: use directory-level `index.md` files for stable structure, local summaries, and links to the relevant docs/code. Then `AGENTS.md` can stay small and only tell the agent how to navigate the documentation before starting a task, and how to update it when the code changes.

For cross-cutting concepts, hierarchy alone is often not enough. A concept can span components, tests, config, migrations, and documentation. I maintain a small convention for that case called `llm-wiki-tags`: it adds explicit `@tag:<slug>` tokens in both code comments and docs, so an agent or a plain text search can find all files related to the same concept: https://github.com/mpashka/llm-wiki-tags

So my answer would be: yes, many small Markdown files are a reasonable direction, but only if you keep them navigable, avoid duplicating the same information in many places, and keep `AGENTS.md` as the entry point rather than the whole knowledge base. Agents can help maintain the docs, but I would still review those updates like code changes.

Q: How do I find which two values in a vector a value falls between in R, and extract the lower one? A:

Convert a, b and x to Date class and sort b since our code will require that. This gives A, B and X. Then use findInterval to perform the search. At the end we check that the result is as expected.

a <- c("2025-04-22", "2025-04-22", "2025-04-29", "2025-6-17", "2025-7-22")
b <- c("2025-04-24", "2025-05-30", "2025-06-25", "2025-04-21", "2025-06-24", "2025-09-26", "2025-04-22")
x <- c("2025-04-21", "2025-04-21", "2025-04-24", "2025-05-30", "2025-06-25")


A <- as.Date(a)
B <- as.Date(sort(b))
X <- as.Date(x)
ix <- findInterval(A, B, left.open = TRUE)
ix <- ifelse(ix == 0, NA, ix) # can omit this line if all elements have match
res <- B[ix]

identical(res, X)
## [1] TRUE

Q: Why `bindkey` in `.zshrc` does not apply unless i source the editor? A:

I have found that the issue is running set -o vi, which resets the bindkey commands I use to fix some of the keys not working as expected. Moving set -o vi to the top fixes the issue.

Q: How to pass request query parameters through a NodeJS application A:

Looks like you're sending a request to the backend API on port 3000 with no query params. In your express.js file you have:

var options = {
method: 'GET',
uri: 'http://localhost:3000/recipes',
json: true
}

Which, as you can see, has NO query parameters. You need to add the params here. If you change this to the code below it should work:

var options = {
method: 'GET',
uri: 'http://localhost:3000/recipes?count=' + req.query.count,
json: true
}

Q: Logstash udp input not working A:
  1. Check logstash log to see what host it opens port on. Default is 0.0.0.0. Which will not be reached. Add "host" parameter in udp definition.
  2. Use port check tool ( like qryport on Windows) to check whether port is actually listened.
